data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: Palau uses the US dollar, so it imports US monetary conditions directly. Inflation was moderate through the 2010s - 9.9% in 2008 on the commodity spike, then a series low of -1.3% in 2016 - before the tourism-collapse-and-reopening cycle produced the sharpest swing in the dataset: 13.2% in 2022 and 12.4% in 2023 on shipping and food costs, collapsing to 3.6% in 2024 and a projected 0.3% in 2025. With no exchange rate or interest-rate lever, Palau's price level is set in Washington and in world commodity markets; the government's only cushion is fiscal.
debt_management: Palau was a low-debt tourism success story - 21.7% of GDP in 2015 - until COVID closed its borders and GDP fell from $0.28bn (2019) to $0.24bn (2021). Borrowing to bridge the collapse drove debt to 52.1% in 2020, 69.9% in 2021 and a series high of 76.4% in 2023. Tourism's return and renewed US Compact funding have brought it down to a projected 62.3% in 2025. The debt is sustainable only because the Compact of Free Association - renewed in 2023 with $889m over 20 years - effectively underwrites the sovereign; without it, Palau's fiscal position would be precarious.

key_events.event: Established the Palau National Marine Sanctuary, closing 80% of its waters to fishing - a conservation landmark.
COVID-19: borders closed and tourism - the economic core - collapsed; Palau stayed virus-free through 2020.
January: Surangel Whipps Jr. inaugurated as president, vowing to keep Taiwan recognition and confront Chinese pressure.
May: signed the renewed Compact of Free Association with the US ($889m over 20 years), enacted March 2024.
November: Whipps re-elected, confirming the pro-US, pro-Taiwan foreign policy line.

outlook_next_decade: The Compact renewal secures the fiscal base through the 2040s, and tourism is recovering - but Palau remains a single-sector economy (high-end diving tourism) in a US-China contest zone, having kept Taiwan recognition while taking Chinese economic pressure. Debt should keep falling if tourism holds. The upside is the marine-sanctuary brand commanding premium tourism; the downside is any renewed border closure or a US aid rethink. Structurally, sovereignty is subsidized - a stable but dependent equilibrium.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
